title: Vivaldi and The Four Seasons
objective: After this level you can explain how Vivaldi painted the seasons in music.
summary: Vivaldi, the Red Priest, wrote about 500 concertos in a fast-slow-fast shape. The Four Seasons (1725) paints scenes from sonnets printed with it: program music. It was little known until 1947.

cards.headline: The Four Seasons was nearly unknown until 1947.
cards.body: It sounds as if it has always been famous. Yet before violinist Louis Kaufman recorded it in 1947, it was virtually unknown, and by then the music was more than two centuries old. What had Vivaldi packed into it that made it catch on so fast?

cards.headline: The Red Priest and his concertos
cards.body: Antonio Vivaldi was a Venetian priest nicknamed "the Red Priest" for his reddish hair. From 1703 he taught violin at the Ospedale della Pietà, a home for foundlings known for training its girls in music. He wrote about 500 concertos and fixed the shape we still expect: three movements, fast, slow, fast. Inside a movement, a refrain for the full orchestra keeps returning between the soloist's showpiece passages.

cards.headline: A concerto that comes with a poem
cards.body: The Four Seasons is four of those violin concertos, one per season, published in 1725. It is scored for solo violin, strings and basso continuo, and its printed parts included one for organ and cello together. Each concerto came with a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, with letters marking where each scene happens. That makes it program music: music set to scenes or a story. You are not just told it's spring; you're shown where the birds come in.

events.label: A harvest feast, then a hunt

mascot.line: Next time Winter plays, listen for the ice. According to the sonnet, somebody is about to fall.

questions.prompt: What makes The Four Seasons an example of program music?

questions.explanation: Each concerto paints the scenes of a sonnet printed with the music, which is what program music does.
